Article Title: Trump wants 'Lake America'. Canada puts up a 24-foot sign saying otherwise
Article Text:
Ontario premier Doug Ford

(with ANI inputs)

In a unique move, Doug Ford, premier of Canada's Ontario province, has put up a large banner along the shores of Lake Ontario, reading “Lake Ontario: Now and Always” in English and French.The move comes in response to US President Donald Trump’s recent decision to "rename" Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.In a video message, Ford described Lake Ontario as a “crown jewel” of both Ontario and Canada."You may have heard President Trump is trying to rename this lake, all because he doesn't like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves."Ford, however, asserted that Lake Ontario has always been known by that name and will continue to be called Lake Ontario."But, let's be serious. Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario and long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario. But just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we've set up this sign to remind them - it's Lake Ontario now and forever," he added.Earlier, Trump signed an executive order directing the US Board on Geographic Names to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.While the executive order applies to American federal mapping agencies, it has no authority over Canadian territory or international hydrographic standards. Canadian leaders across party lines, along with US state officials, have largely dismissed or rejected the change.The order followed a similar move last year by the Trump administration to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America."Lake Ontario is one of the five Great Lakes, which straddle the border between the two neighbouring countries.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has already rejected Trump's "renaming" of Lake Ontario to “Lake America."US state officials, including New York governor Kathy Hochul, whose state borders the lake, said they would not adopt the new name, calling the move "absurd" amid pressing economic and trade concerns for agricultural exporters.Indigenous leaders, including Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard, condemned the renaming as an "attempt to erase historical and cultural roots."
Article Summary: Doug Ford, premier of Canada's Ontario province, has put up a large banner along the shores of Lake Ontario, reading “Lake Ontario: Now and Always” in English and French. The move comes in response to US President Donald Trump’s recent decision to "rename" Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’

Article Title: Russia prepares for ‘massive strikes’ against Ukraine's energy facilities
Article Text:
Russia claimed the preparations are in response to Ukraine's repeated attacks.

Russian forces have begun preparations for what Moscow described as “massive strikes” against Ukraine’s energy facilities in response to attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure and the country’s energy sector, Russia’s Defence Ministry said Sunday.The ministry said Russian forces had also continued overnight to carry out coordinated strikes against facilities linked to Ukraine’s defence industry, reported Reuters.The latest warning comes a day after a Russian strike on Ukraine’s Bucha district near Kyiv killed at least 37 people, according to Ukrainian officials. The attack damaged at least 50 residential buildings and triggered a large fire that spread to several homes and a restaurant, officials said.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a warehouse in the village of Myla was hit and followed by an explosion. He said authorities had opened criminal proceedings over suspected official negligence, alleging that ammunition had been stored near residential areas despite regulations prohibiting it.The attack came as Kyiv faced a third consecutive day of near-continuous Russian air raids, disrupting daily life and economic activity in the capital.Russia’s latest threat raises the prospect of further attacks on Ukraine’s power infrastructure, which has repeatedly been targeted during the more than four-year-old war. Both sides have increasingly used long-range missiles and drones to strike military, energy and infrastructure targets far behind the front lines.Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and the conflict has since evolved into a prolonged war marked by repeated aerial attacks, territorial battles and strikes on critical infrastructure.
Article Summary: Russian forces have begun preparations for'massive strikes' on Ukraine's energy facilities. Russia claims the preparations are in response to attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure and the country's energy sector. The latest warning comes a day after a Russian strike on Ukraine’s Bucha district near Kyiv killed at least 37 people.

Article Title: He is turning 100, so his community wants to give him 100 birthday cards: Texas WWII veteran’s remarkable century is being celebrated with a heartfelt tribute
Article Text:
Mr. Weldon Bowen

c/o Watkins-Logan Texas State Veterans Home

11466 Honour Lane

Tyler, TX 75708

A Texas World War II veteran is preparing to celebrate a remarkable milestone, and his community wants to make sure he receives 100 reasons to smile on his 100th birthday. Weldon Kenneth Bowen, a resident of the Watkins-Logan Texas State Veterans Home in Tyler, Texas, will turn 100 on September 5. To mark the occasion, the Texas Veterans Land Board has launched an appeal encouraging people to send birthday cards to Bowen as part of its “100 for 100” initiative, as per a PEOPLE report.According to a press release from Texas General Land Office Commissioner Dawn Buckingham, M.D., the programme is aimed at celebrating veterans who reach their centennial birthdays. The initiative brings together communities to honour their service and lives by helping them receive at least 100 birthday cards.For Bowen, the celebration is a tribute not only to a century of life but also to his service in the US Marine Corps during the closing months of World War II. Born in Luling, Texas, Bowen enlisted in the Marine Corps shortly after graduating from high school. He officially joined the service on August 3, 1945, as World War II was drawing to a close.After completing basic training, Bowen was stationed at the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard in Bremerton, Washington.His service came during a pivotal period in American history, as the war in the Pacific was coming to an end.Bowen remained in the Marine Corps until August 1946, when he was honourably discharged. During his time in uniform, he earned the Good Conduct Medal and was recognised as an Expert Rifleman.Nearly 80 years after leaving the Marines, Bowen is now set to celebrate his 100th birthday surrounded by a community that wants to recognise the life he has lived and the service he once gave to his country.The “100 for 100” campaign is asking Texans, as well as others who would like to participate, to send Bowen a birthday greeting. The idea is simple: 100 cards for a veteran turning 100.For those who may never have met Bowen, a handwritten birthday card offers a small but meaningful way to connect with someone whose life spans an extraordinary chapter of American history. Each message can serve as a reminder that his military service and century-long journey have not been forgotten.People interested in sending Bowen a birthday card can mail their wishes to:As Bowen approaches his 100th birthday on September 5, the campaign is hoping that cards will arrive from across Texas and beyond, turning an ordinary birthday greeting into a collective celebration of a remarkable life.
Article Summary: Weldon Kenneth Bowen, a resident of the Watkins-Logan Texas State Veterans Home in Tyler, Texas, will turn 100 on September 5. The Texas Veterans Land Board has launched an appeal encouraging people to send birthday cards to Bowen as part of its “100 for 100” initiative.

Article Title: NASA has tested a navigation system that lets satellites determine where they are without GPS by treating other spacecraft and debris as landmarks, while refining more than 200 object orbits in three
Article Text:
Starling tested GPS-free navigation using onboard cameras to track space objects. (Credit: NASA)

How FALCON uses space objects as landmarks

First demonstration of its kind

From University research to space test

NASA has tested a navigation system that allows satellites to determine their position without relying on GPS. Instead of depending on an external navigation network, the system uses other spacecraft and orbital debris as reference points to work out where a satellite is in space.The technology, called FALCON, was tested as part of NASA’s Starling mission. FALCON stands for Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation. According to Science Daily, during the demonstration, the system not only helped a spacecraft determine its own orbit but also improved the estimated orbits of more than 200 other space objects in just three days.The test is aimed at making spacecraft more independent. GPS signals that satellites use near Earth can become weak, unreliable or unavailable around the Moon and in deep space. A system that allows spacecraft to navigate using objects they can observe could therefore support missions that cannot depend on GPS.The FALCON experiment used Starling’s onboard cameras and a catalogue of known satellites and other space objects. The cameras, which are also used for tracking stars, observed objects around the spacecraft. FALCON then compared those observations with information in a publicly available catalogue of known space objects maintained by the US Department of War.FALCON uses objects already present in orbit as reference points. These can include other spacecraft and pieces of orbital debris. Once the system identifies and verifies the objects seen by Starling’s cameras, it can use their known positions to calculate Starling’s own orbit.This means the spacecraft does not have to depend entirely on navigation information sent from outside. Instead, it can use what its cameras observe around it to help determine where it is.The system was also tested for another task: improving information about the objects it observes. Mission controllers loaded a catalogue containing about 20,000 space objects and their predicted orbits onto Starling.FALCON then compared the predicted information in that catalogue with measurements collected by Starling’s cameras. From those measurements, it calculated Starling’s position while also refining the estimated locations of other objects.The results showed that the updated estimates could be more precise than the existing catalogue information. Over three days, FALCON improved the known orbits of more than 200 objects without requiring intervention from operators on the ground.NASA said FALCON’s ability to determine a spacecraft’s own orbit using optical cameras and its position relative to other objects represents a first for this type of spacecraft navigation.The experiment also showed that Starling could produce improved predictions of where observed objects would be compared with information supplied by ground stations. This could be useful for missions in which spacecraft need to operate with less dependence on Earth-based systems.“FALCON is yet another success for the Starling demonstration mission. The results from FALCON can have far-reaching implications for on-orbit space-traffic monitoring, collision avoidance, and alternative navigation,” said Roger Hunter, programme manager for NASA’s Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems programme at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley.The ability to navigate independently could become important as NASA works on missions farther from Earth. The agency said the technology could support lunar satellite swarms, distributed science missions and future human exploration.Precise positioning is particularly important for distributed science missions. In these missions, several spacecraft can collect measurements from different locations, making accurate knowledge of their positions necessary to align and use those measurements properly.Autonomous navigation could also have a role in space-traffic management. If spacecraft can determine their positions and update information about objects around them, they could reduce some dependence on ground-based tracking networks while supporting collision avoidance.FALCON was developed through a joint flight experiment between NASA and EraDrive, a startup that emerged from Stanford University. The system combines EraDrive’s Era-Core flight software and embedded algorithms with Starling’s cameras and its onboard catalogue of known satellites.The work originally began as a University SmallSat Technology Partnerships project. It later developed into EraDrive, which is commercialising its Era-Core software and related hardware for wider use.Starling provided an opportunity to test the technology in actual space conditions. The demonstration showed how flight software and onboard observations can be combined to give spacecraft greater autonomy.The testing is not finished yet. Later this year, Starling is expected to expand the FALCON experiment using Era-Core. The mission’s four spacecraft will share tracking information with one another and use the combined observations to refine their positions collectively.NASA’s Ames Research Center leads the Starling mission. NASA’s Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems programme, based at Ames and part of the Research and Technology Mission Directorate, funds and manages the mission.
Article Summary: The technology, called FALCON, was tested as part of NASA’s Starling mission. It uses other spacecraft and orbital debris as reference points to work out where a satellite is in space. The test is aimed at making spacecraft more independent. GPS signals that satellites use near Earth can become weak or unreliable.

Article Title: Nepal-Tibet floods: 750 dead, 20,000 deployed as rising rivers hamper rescue ops - top developments
Article Text:
A drone view shows people walking on a mud-covered road next to damaged houses following deadly flash floods and mudslides in Nepal (Reuters photo)

Fresh flood warnings issued as river levels rise

Rescue focus shifts to people trapped in hydropower tunnels

Over 8,000 rescued as nearly 20,000 security personnel deployed

8,399 Nepal Army personnel

7,293 Nepal Police personnel

4,203 Armed Police Force Nepal personnel

Nepal seeks DNA testing and forensic support to identify bodies

India sends fourth relief flight carrying 11 tonnes of supplies

More than 2,400 people missing in Nepal, including foreigners

New lake threat eases, but another landslide creates fresh risk

Infrastructure damage leaves communities cut off

International assistance continues

Nepal's LGBTQ+ community holds candlelight vigil

The death toll from the catastrophic floods that struck Nepal and China's Tibet this week has risen to 750, while more than 3,000 people remain missing, as authorities warned of possible fresh flooding and rescuers continued operations in difficult conditions.The disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse on Wednesday, unleashing torrents of ice, rock, mud and debris through Himalayan river systems. The floods devastated settlements, destroyed bridges and roads, and damaged hydropower infrastructure across the affected areas.As of the latest updates on Sunday, 734 people were confirmed dead in Nepal, while 2,498 people remained missing, according to Nepal's disaster authorities.On the Chinese side in Tibet, authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, taking the combined missing toll to more than 3,000.Here are the top developments from the disaster:Nepalese authorities warned residents in flood-hit districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River on Sunday.Flood warning notices were sent to people's phones as rescue teams continued efforts to clear damaged sections of the highway linking Kathmandu with some of the worst-hit areas.The warnings came after Chinese authorities informed Nepal that water flow had increased upstream, Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told news agency AP.The NDRRMA also warned rescue and relief personnel in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and surrounding areas to exercise caution as the flow in the Bhote Koshi River increased further.Fresh rain also caused water levels in the Trishuli River to rise, prompting residents and rescue workers to move to higher ground, Reuters reported.Rescue operations are increasingly focused on hundreds of people believed to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower projects after the floods swept through the region.Nepal has sought specialised international assistance for tunnel rescue operations. Foreign ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said the country did not require foreign help for general rescue operations but needed support in areas including tunnel rescue, DNA testing, refrigerated storage of bodies and forensic identification.Indian and Chinese experts are assisting efforts to open tunnels.Nepal foreign minister Shisir Khanal told news agency ANI that more than 4,000 people had been rescued over the previous three days and that specialised teams had arrived to assist with tunnel rescue operations.According to the NDRRMA, 279 people, including 227 foreign nationals, have been rescued by helicopter from a hydropower tunnel.Nepal's disaster authority said 8,186 people have so far been rescued.The rescue effort has involved 19,895 security personnel, including:The NDRRMA said 2,974 people were rescued by the Nepal Army, 2,699 by Nepal Police and 2,513 by the Armed Police Force Nepal.The disaster has also left 242 people injured, while surgical medical teams have been deployed in affected areas.Authorities are seeking specialised forensic assistance to identify the hundreds of bodies recovered from the disaster zone."We are seeking additional support for forensic laboratories. We have found more than 600 bodies, many of them in very difficult conditions to identify. We need to conduct rapid DNA analysis," foreign minister Khanal said.Unidentified bodies recovered during rescue operations have been kept across 21 hospitals in various districts, according to the NDRRMA.The latest Indian assistance includes forensic experts equipped to support DNA analysis.India has sent a fourth flight to Kathmandu carrying relief supplies and specialised technical assistance for Nepal's rescue operations.External affairs minister S Jaishankar said the flight brought "essential supplies and technical capabilities" to support ongoing rescue and relief efforts.According to the Indian Embassy in Nepal, the aircraft carried 11 tonnes of relief material, including a tunnel technical team, forensic experts for DNA analysis, blankets, sleeping bags, tarpaulins, plastic sheets and hygiene kits.Foreign minister Khanal said four Indian flights carrying relief supplies had arrived in Nepal and expressed gratitude for India's assistance.Of the 2,419 people reported missing or out of contact in an earlier NDRRMA update, 589 were foreign nationals, while 127 were Nepalis accompanying foreign tourists.The missing included 933 people linked to hydropower projects, with 562 missing in Rasuwa and 115 in Nuwakot.On the Tibetan side, authorities said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were among those missing, according to Reuters. They included 104 Nepalis, 49 Indians, 33 Latvians, 18 Americans and 15 Britons.Rescue operations have repeatedly been disrupted by bad weather and concerns over a lake that formed across the Nepal-China border after the glacier collapse.The lake had largely drained by Saturday evening, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.However, drones later detected a landslide 2.8 km downstream of the lake, creating another dam and a fresh pool of water. Authorities moved rescue personnel near the Gyirong border crossing to safety.China and Nepal are continuing to monitor water levels and other potential hazards in the disaster zone.The floods destroyed large concrete and suspension bridges, leaving communities on opposite sides of rivers cut off from each other.Homes and businesses that survived the initial flooding remained without electricity in some areas, with damaged power poles and wires lying in the mud.The Prithivi Highway, a key route for food, fuel and other supplies entering Kathmandu, remained operational in large parts, although some sections continued to require repairs.The Nepal government has released cash assistance, including NPR 10 million each for Rasuwa and Nuwakot, NPR 5 million for Dhading and NPR 67.5 million for 15 local municipalities.Authorities have also dispatched 37 trucks carrying food and non-food relief materials, while helicopter flights have been used to transport supplies to affected areas.International assistance for Nepal's flood response is continuing, with India, China, the United States and Malaysia extending support.India has sent four flights carrying relief supplies and specialised technical assistance. The fourth flight carried 11 tonnes of relief material, including a tunnel technical team and forensic experts for DNA analysis.The United States has provided more than $3.6 million in humanitarian assistance, including emergency food support for up to 10,000 flood-affected households, the US Embassy in Kathmandu said on Sunday.The assistance also includes emergency supplies, while the US is coordinating with the Nepal government and humanitarian organisations on further support.Malaysia on Sunday said it would send a specialised disaster search-and-rescue team to Nepal and provide $1 million in financial aid.China has mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220 million yuan ($32.7 million) for relief efforts.Beijing is also providing emergency aid, relief supplies, satellite and hydrological data and tunnel rescue experts to Nepal.Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi told his Nepalese counterpart that the disaster was the countries' "most severe cross-border disaster" in recent years.Members of Nepal's LGBTQ+ community gathered in Kathmandu on Saturday for a candlelight vigil to honour those killed and pray for people still missing.The event was organised by the Blue Diamond Society, which cancelled its planned Nepal Pride Parade and GaiJatra Celebration in view of the disaster."We organised this small gathering to light candles and pray for the eternal peace of all who lost their lives in this disaster, and to pray that those who are still missing are found as quickly as possible," a community member told news agency PTI.
Article Summary: Death toll from Nepal floods rises to 750, while more than 3,000 people remain missing. Fresh flood warnings issued as river levels rise. Rescue focus shifts to people trapped in hydropower tunnels. India sends fourth relief flight carrying 11 tonnes of supplies.

Article Title: American startup raises $180 million to drill rock over 5km deep to build world's first superhot geothermal plant at 500 °C
Article Text:
Vaporising a rock without touching it

Why a superhot rock

A previous experiment

Quaise Energy, an American startup, announced on August 27 the final closing of a $180 million funding round, which included $35 million from Nabors, to finance the Obsidian Project in Oregon, where a microwave gyrotron will create wells in rock between 300 °C and 500 °C to establish the first commercial superhot geothermal plant on the planet, as per a report by ThinkGeoEnergy.According to the statement, the Series B totals $180 million, bringing the startup's total funding to $280 million since its inception. The first tranche, amounting to $134 million, was previously announced on July 7, led by Prelude Ventures with participation from Japanese companies JERA and Idemitsu Kosan. The new addition to the list is Nabors Industries, one of the largest oil and gas drillers in the world, which contributed $35 million and signed a strategic agreement. According to the release, Nabors will provide a dedicated land rig and integrate its reservoir modelling platform, well design, and drilling strategy into the project. In other words, the oil and gas industry is lending a rig, software, and personnel for a technology that promises to eliminate the need for a drill bit.A gyrotron is a millimetre-wave generator, a high-frequency microwave technology created to heat plasma in nuclear fusion reactors.According to MIT News, engineer Paul Woskov from MIT’s Plasma Science and Fusion Centre spent 14 years testing the concept of directing this beam downwards. His description is straightforward: these are very powerful beam sources, akin to lasers, but at a different frequency range.In practice, the beam travels down a waveguide to the bottom of the well, heating the rock to the point of melting and vaporising it without mechanical contact. There is no rotating drill bit or carbide teeth wearing away. The company defines the process as rock ablation with zero contact, and that’s where the advantage lies. The deeper you go, the hotter and harder the rock becomes; this is precisely where traditional drilling begins to fail.According to Quaise’s July update, the company drilled over 100 meters of granite at a test site in Central Texas, and is now approaching 1 kilometre in depth at the same location, which it refers to as the deepest feat achieved by contactless drilling. The leap from there to more than 5 km in Oregon is substantial, and the company acknowledges this in its timeline.Traditional geothermal energy works with hot water or steam at moderate temperatures, near volcanoes or geological fault lines. The thesis of superhot geothermal energy is different: to descend to where rock exceeds 374 °C and water reaches a supercritical state, which carries far more energy per kilogram than regular steam. Thus, a single superhot well can deliver several times what a conventional geothermal well produces. Quaise targets rock at temperatures between 300 °C and 500 °C and at depths that, in most parts of the world, exceed 5 km.What makes Oregon special is the gradient. According to ThinkGeoEnergy, the area leased by Quaise lies south of the Newberry volcano, right next to the border of the Newberry National Volcanic Monument. It spans 1,334 acres within the Deschutes National Forest, featuring a geothermal gradient of about 100 °C per kilometre. In other words, temperatures that elsewhere would require 10 kilometres of drilling are found there at a fraction of the depth. The target reservoirs for Phase I are described at 315 °C and 365 °C.The plan published in April outlines two sets of wells, each with one injector and two producers, and two generating units connected side by side. Phase I is set to deliver 50 MW, with power expected on the grid by 2030; Phase II aims for 250 MW, with the company discussing gigawatt-scale in the long term. For now, the initial wells employ conventional drilling to penetrate the surface layer; the gyrotron will only come into play when the goal is the hotter basement rock at 365 °C, as Quaise explained to the publication.For Brazil, the interesting development is Nabors’ entry. The drilling company operates rigs in various markets, and the combination of a conventional rig for the shallow part with a gyrotron for the hot section is a model that could operate in any sedimentary basin with a favourable gradient, without relying on a volcano. The country hardly explores geothermal energy, partly because there is little hot rock near the surface. If the technology proves successful, depth will no longer be an obstacle, and what will matter is having the rig, team, and regulations ready.Anthony Petrello, president and CEO of Nabors, summarised the logic in the statement by saying that millimetre wave technology changes the equation by reaching superhot rocks at depths beyond the reach of conventional methods. Carlos Araque, CEO and president of Quaise, spoke about unlocking the world’s most powerful clean energy source.A discussion about deep drilling inevitably references the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia. Soviet scientists began in 1970 and reached 12,262 meters by 1989, making it the deepest hole ever drilled, with just a 23-centimetre diameter. What halted progress was not the rock, but the heat. Temperatures at the bottom exceeded 180 °C, well above what models predicted. Under those conditions, the rock behaved more like plastic than solid. The project was abandoned in 1994 due to lack of funds and drill bits capable of withstanding the conditions.It’s clear why the idea of vaporising rock instead of scraping it generates such interest. Kola took nearly two decades to traverse 12 kilometres in still relatively cool rock. Quaise aims to work in rock three times hotter, arguing that millimetre waves are unaffected by the target’s hardness or temperature. It’s a bold promise, and the company still needs to prove that the beam remains stable and efficient well beyond Texas tests.
Article Summary: Quaise Energy, an American startup, announced on August 27 the final closing of a $180 million funding round. Nabors Industries, one of the largest oil and gas drillers in the world, contributed $35 million and signed a strategic agreement. A microwave gyrotron will create wells in rock between 300 °C and 500 °C to establish the first commercial superhot geothermal plant on the planet. The company defines the process as rock ablation with zero contact.

Article Title: A Colombian man struggling to build his own home helped create Lego-like bricks from recycled plastic; by 2015 the system was sheltering 42 displaced families and could build a 40-sq-m home in 5 days
Article Text:
Houses with recycled plastic bricks in Colombia

Four people can build a house in five days

How Plastic waste helps buildings

A worker assembles blocks made from recycled plastic to build a house in Colombia.

Designed to cost less

Addressing concerns about plastic homes

A Colombian architect has developed a construction system that turns discarded plastic and rubber into blocks for temporary and permanent homes. The blocks can be assembled and dismantled like lego without glue, cement or water, offering a cheaper alternative to traditional construction in rural areas.Fernando Llanos, who had been trying to build his own house but faced difficulties transporting construction materials to his property in Cundinamarca. He eventually began exploring plastic as an alternative building material.The project was developed by Conceptos Plasticos. According to Extrusiones SA's report, the company’s system uses industrial plastic as well as plastic collected from ordinary consumers. Different types of plastic are mixed depending on the properties required for a building. The finished blocks are made through extrusion, in which the plastic is melted and poured into moulds. The blocks were designed for one and two-storey homes, with major elements such as walls and beams made from recycled plastic.One of the main features of the system is that the houses can be assembled and taken apart. In an interview with Semana Sustainable, architect Oscar Andres Mendez explained how the process works.“Four people can build a 40-square-metre house in five days and take it apart in three days. The houses are transferable, meaning they can be moved anywhere. The blocks fit together, so there is no need for glue, cement or water, just a hammer and a wrench.”The company had already used the system for temporary shelters for people displaced by violence. In 2015, it built a shelter for 42 families in Guapi, Cauca. The design was adapted for mobility and local weather conditions, with the recycled plastic blocks allowing the shelters to be dismantled and moved elsewhere within the municipality.By the time of the interview, three shelters in Guapi, each covering 400 square metres and housing 242 displaced people in total were also built. Some houses in Valle del Cauca had been purchased by private individuals, while the company had also exported its products to Costa Rica. It was also preparing to inaugurate 10 houses in Cartagena.The company does not use just one kind of plastic. Mendez said it works with industrial plastic and material that has passed through consumers' hands. The company buys plastic from businesses and some groups of recyclers.“Each type of plastic gives the product different properties. Some provide flexibility, while others provide rigidity, and so on. Once we have defined the design and the needs of the house we want to build, we mix several types of plastic,” Mendez said.Developing the right formula was not simple. Used plastic behaves differently from new material and required more experimentation before the blocks could be produced.Mendez said, “Working with virgin plastic is simple because there are defined parameters, but used plastic requires more experimentation.”The company holds patents for the blocks and said it was the only manufacturer of them in Colombia and abroad at the time.The blocks undergo treatment intended to make them fire-resistant. The plastic structure can also make buildings resistant to earthquakes.Cost is another part of the project's appeal. The construction is 30 per cent cheaper than traditional systems in rural areas.The use of recycled material is also intended to reduce the amount of plastic sent to landfills. The project said it could lower water and energy consumption and CO2 emissions through the use of recycled materials.For Mendez, however, the project was about more than construction and waste management. He wanted recycling to be linked directly with housing.“At the moment, we have a major project in which we want to promote education further. Although we were already visiting schools and giving talks, we want citizens to realise that simply separating their waste and taking it to a nearby collection point can help provide someone with decent housing.”He described the work as one that 'closes the plastic cycle', connecting an environmental problem with a social need.The idea of living in a house made from waste can raise concerns about safety and health. Mendez said people often associate a plastic house with bags or a tent rather than a solid building material.“When we say, ‘this is a plastic house’, people imagine bags or something like a tent. They never think about hard materials such as soft-drink bottle caps or paint cans, which are also made of plastic.”He said people's reactions often changed after they saw the blocks and understood how the plastic was transformed.Health was another common question. Mendez said people asked whether living in houses made from waste could cause illnesses or allergies.He explained that the material goes through temperatures above 300 degrees, which it said ensures the death of microorganisms. It also worked with clean plastics that had already gone through grinding and washing before reaching the company.
Article Summary: A Colombian architect has developed a construction system that turns discarded plastic and rubber into blocks for temporary and permanent homes. The blocks can be assembled and dismantled like lego without glue, cement or water, offering a cheaper alternative to traditional construction in rural areas. The company had already used the system for temporary shelters for people displaced by violence.

Article Title: Everest veterans, mountain guides enter choked hydropower tunnel to rescue 6
Article Text:
Search and rescue operations under way in Rasuwa

TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT, NEPAL): Everest veterans and some of Nepal's most highly trained mountain guides joined rescue operations in flood-ravaged Rasuwa, with a specialist team entering a mud-choked hydropower tunnel Saturday and pushing around 120m inside before thick sludge and debris blocked further movement. The deployment brought skills normally used on Himalayan expeditions - rope fixing, cliff access, helicopter longline operations and movement through unstable terrain - into parts of the disaster zone where roads had disappeared and conventional rescue methods were proving difficult.The team entered the tunnel at Chilime hydropower project, where six people were believed to be inside. IFMGA-certified guide Ashish Gurung, Dorjee Sherpa and veteran climber Jenjen Lama moved into the tunnel using rope protection and fixed lines before chest-deep sludge stopped them. They recovered a camera bag during the search and concluded that pumps and excavation equipment would be needed before rescuers could safely move deeper.The Chilime search formed part of a much larger tunnel rescue challenge across the flood-hit hydropower corridor. Six people were believed trapped inside the Chilime tunnel, while at Upper Trishuli-1 around 300 workers were believed to remain inside its tunnel system.The affected workforce across the projects included Nepalese, Indian, Chinese and South Korean nationals, with authorities still reconciling project attendance records and rescue lists to establish exactly how many remained trapped or uncontactable.Lama, a veteran high-altitude guide, has summited Mount Everest six times and Ama Dablam 12 times, besides climbing Lhotse and Manaslu. Another climber in the wider operation was Dawa Jangbu Sherpa, a guide with more than two decades of mountaineering experience.The specialist contingent also included Dawa Singhi Hyolmo, an IFMGA-certified international mountain guide and national mountaineering instructor with more than a decade of high-altitude experience, and fellow IFMGA-certified guides Man Raj Gurung and Ashish Gurung. Pemba Wangchu Sherpa, Bikram Karki, Sabin Thakuri, Geshman Tamang, Sandesh Sherpa and Chhiring Sherpa were among other trained climbers and rescuers mobilised.NNMGA and Nepal Mountaineering Instructors Association deployed helicopter longline and ground teams after floods swept away roads and bridges and left parts of Rasuwa accessible only across steep slopes, cliffs and unstable ground.
Article Summary: Everest veterans join rescue operations in flood-ravaged Rasuwa. Specialist team enters a mud-choked hydropower tunnel. Six people believed trapped inside the Chilime tunnel. Around 300 workers believed to remain inside Upper Trishuli-1.

Article Title: Kim Jong UN shakes up North Korea’s military, dismisses defence minister No Kwang Chol
Article Text:
North Korea's Kim Jong Un shakes up military; names Kim Song Gi as the new defence minister

Trilateral drills set to continue

North Korea has dismissed its defence minister No Kwang Chol in a reshuffle of the country’s top military leadership, state media reported Sunday, with leader Kim Jong Un approving the changes at a meeting on Saturday.The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said the changes were part of “structural reorganization plans”.No Kwang Chol was removed as defence minister and demoted within the ruling party to “first vice-director of the Munitions Industry Department”. Kim Song Gi, head of the General Political Bureau of the Korean People's Army, was appointed the new defence minister.Defence adviser Pak Jong Chon was named vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission and elevated to the ruling party's Political Bureau. Several other senior officials were also promoted.The reshuffle came as Kim praised scientists, researchers and officials for advances in military technology at a ceremony on Saturday.KCNA said the recipients had helped “resolving scientific and technological problems of epochal significance in developing new combat weapon systems”. It did not specify the systems involved, as reported by AFP.North Korea's weapons research centre had also recently developed “exclusive technologies, to be regarded as an event in strengthening the capability for fighting a war”, KCNA said.The report did not provide details but said the advances demonstrated “the course of unique development of the country's military and technological capabilities”.In late June, Kim oversaw tests of a new extended-range multiple rocket launcher and artillery system.The leadership reshuffle follows the conclusion of annual military exercises between South Korea and the US, which Pyongyang routinely condemns as invasion preparations.The drills were shortened this year after US President Donald Trump ordered them cut short. Trump has called the exercises provocative towards North Korea and criticised Seoul for not supporting his war against Iran.Trump has also praised Kim, whom he met twice during his first term, and expressed interest in another meeting, potentially this year. North Korea has shown little sign of reciprocating, continuing missile tests and condemning the drills.Pyongyang has also criticised US arms sales to South Korea and Washington's plans to fund programmes documenting human rights abuses in North Korea.Meanwhile, South Korea, the US and Japan are set to hold trilateral Freedom Edge exercises from September 7 to 11 in international waters east and south of South Korea's Jeju Island.Seoul's joint chiefs of staff described the exercise as “a defensive drill conducted annually by the three countries to respond to North Korea's nuclear and missile threats and safeguard peace and stability in the region.”
Article Summary: No Kwang Chol was removed as defence minister and demoted within the ruling party. Kim Song Gi, head of the General Political Bureau of the Korean People's Army, was appointed the new defence minister. South Korea, the US and Japan are set to hold trilateral Freedom Edge exercises from September 7 to 11.

Article Title: A Houston lawyer bought a 15,000-sq-ft mansion listed for $15.5 million just to demolish it; he plans to donate about $4 million of its materials and turn the land into a garden
Article Text:
Houston attorney Tony Buzbee and his wife, Frances, recently acquired 1708 River Oaks Blvd

Salvaging luxury fixtures for charity

Property value and River Oaks history

A history of high-profile property moves

Creating a larger private garden

Prominent Houston trial lawyer Tony Buzbee has bought a 15,000-square-foot luxury mansion listed for $15.5 million in the exclusive River Oaks neighbourhood, with plans to tear down the entire house and turn the property into a private garden estate. The purchase of 1708 River Oaks Boulevard allows Buzbee and his wife, Frances Moody Buzbee, to expand their existing property directly beside their long-time home at 1722 River Oaks Boulevard. Instead of living in or renovating the large mansion, the couple has partnered with Habitat for Humanity to remove and save usable materials from the property before demolition begins.Reports from the Houston Business Journal and the Houston Chronicle confirmed that the non-profit will manage the salvage work, recovering millions of pounds of architectural fittings and building materials to support affordable housing projects across Texas. “They will be tearing it down and salvaging approximately $4 million worth of high-end materials, appliances, air units and the like for their mission,” Buzbee said in an email statement about the donation. “They are excited to have it, and we are proud to support them.”Under the agreement with Habitat for Humanity, salvage crews will carefully remove materials from inside and outside the 15,000-square-foot mansion before the site is cleared.The recovery work will include high-end kitchen equipment, custom woodwork, marble fittings, large air-conditioning units and other building materials. The donated materials are estimated to be worth $4 million. Habitat for Humanity plans to use some of the recovered items in affordable housing projects, while specialised fixtures may be sold through its ReStore shops to raise money for its work. Once the house is removed, the property will become a large private garden. The new green space will connect directly with the family’s main home next door, effectively doubling the size of their landscaped grounds along one of Houston’s best-known streets.The purchase reflects continued activity in River Oaks, an 1,100-acre master-planned community founded in 1924 by brothers Will and Mike Hogg and Hugh Potter. The neighbourhood remains one of Houston’s most exclusive residential areas and is controlled by strict deed restrictions and private maintenance rules overseen by the River Oaks Property Owners association. Harris Central Appraisal District records reviewed by Zillow show that 1708 River Oaks Boulevard had an assessed value of $18,062,181 in 2026. Official tax records show that the property had an annual tax bill of $383,861 before the sale. The $15.5 million asking price was therefore considerably below the official assessed value. Real estate publication The Real Deal said the purchase fits a growing trend known as landmaxxing. The term describes wealthy homeowners buying neighbouring properties, removing existing buildings and combining the lots into larger private estates.Buzbee, a former United States Marine Corps officer who ran for Houston mayor in 2019, has had a prominent presence on River Oaks Boulevard since buying his first home at 1722 River Oaks Boulevard for $14 million in 2013. In 2017, Buzbee drew widespread attention after buying a fully operational, demilitarised $600,000 World War II Sherman tank that had taken part in the Normandy landings. He parked the tank along the kerb outside his home, leading to a dispute with the local property owners association. He eventually donated the tank to Texas A&M University in 2018. The main estate also became the scene of a major police investigation in 2019 after burglars broke into the home following a Super Bowl event. They stole $21 million worth of artwork, jewellery, firearms and electronics. The items were later recovered after Buzbee offered a $50,000 reward for information that led to arrests. In February 2022, the couple put their 12,209-square-foot Tudor-style mansion on the market for $27.5 million through Douglas Elliman Real Estate. PaperCity Magazine and CultureMap Houston reported at the time that the listing even allowed buyers to pay in Bitcoin. When the home failed to sell at that price, the family decided to keep it and expand onto the neighbouring property instead.The demolition of 1708 River Oaks Boulevard will remove a mansion that included six bedrooms, an indoor swimming pool, a domed stained-glass ceiling, a lacquered library, a wine vault and a wellness wing with a beauty salon. Removing a fully functioning estate of this size is one of the more notable residential site clearances in recent Texas real estate. The work will happen in stages, starting with Habitat for Humanity’s salvage operation. Once workers have removed all usable fixtures and mechanical equipment, heavy machinery will bring down the remaining structure. Landscaping crews will then begin work on the garden extension. The finished project will join the two River Oaks lots into one large, connected green property. The expansion will give the family more privacy while directing millions of dollars worth of reusable construction materials to charitable housing projects. Share your thoughts on the story in the comments.
Article Summary: Houston attorney Tony Buzbee and his wife, Frances, recently acquired 1708 River Oaks Blvd. The couple has partnered with Habitat for Humanity to remove and save usable materials from the property before demolition begins. The recovery work will include high-end kitchen equipment, custom woodwork, marble fittings, large air-conditioning units and other building materials. The donated materials are estimated to be worth $4 million.

Article Title: A Mexican entrepreneur began melting discarded plastic into wall and roof panels; within three years his startup had built 500 rooms and secured contracts for 300 homes
Article Text:
An entrepreneur began melting discarded plastic into walls

Turning waste into building panels

Affordable homes through local governments

Better pay for informal waste collectors

Taking the model beyond Puebla

Workers at a recycling plant in central Mexico are turning five and a half tonnes of discarded plastic bottles and old toys every day into strong building materials, helping low-income families get better homes while keeping waste out of local dumps. The process, developed in 2013 by social enterprise EcoDom in Puebla state, turns melted plastic waste into strong wall and roofing panels. Within three years of starting operations, the company had built 500 rooms for municipal housing programmes and won public contracts to construct 300 complete homes across nearby towns. A report by media organisation Unreasonable Group explains how founder Carlos Daniel González created the company to tackle two problems at the same time: pollution and a serious shortage of affordable housing. González grew up in Puebla, where government figures and regional data cited by Unreasonable Group show that 64 per cent of people live in poverty. He saw the effects of unmanaged waste around him from an early age. “As a kid, I remember seeing all of the plastic and the contamination it caused, for us and for the animals,” said González. “I've always cared about the environment, so I decided I had to create and lead a solution.”Mexico is the world’s 12th-largest consumer of plastic and produces more than five million tonnes of plastic waste each year. The World Bank estimates that 11.5 million Mexicans live in extreme poverty on $1.25 or less a day, leaving many people without safe and basic housing. “I live in a place with a lot of poverty and problems of marginalization,” said González. “Some people live in truly deplorable conditions, places you can't even call houses. My vision is very clear. I have the conviction to help the most people I can have a dignified life by getting rid of extreme poverty, cleaning up my country at the same time.” To make the building panels, workers collect different types of used plastic and sort them to remove materials that could release toxic fumes when heated. A machine then cuts the selected plastic into small, even pieces before workers place them in industrial ovens heated to 350 degrees Celsius. After 30 minutes in the oven, the melted plastic is moved into a hydraulic press. The machine compresses the material and turns it into solid panels measuring about 2.4 metres long, 1.2 metres wide and 2.5 centimetres thick. The Puebla factory produces 120 panels a day, recycling tonnes of waste that would otherwise likely end up in landfills. A complete 40-square-metre home needs 80 panels and includes two bedrooms, a bathroom, a living area and a kitchen. “It only takes seven days to build a house that uses two tons of plastic,” said González. He also pointed to the strength and other benefits of the finished material, saying: “[A house] keeps you warm, the costs are low, it's great for the environment, and it will last 100 years without falling apart. These are just some of our value propositions.”EcoDom does not work only as a private construction company. It supplies building panels directly to local governments and non-governmental organisations involved in subsidised social housing programmes. Prices recorded by Unreasonable Group show that roof panels cost 600 Mexican pesos ($33), exterior wall panels cost 650 pesos ($36), and interior panels cost 500 pesos ($28). Through government housing programmes, eligible low-income families pay about 5,000 pesos ($280) for a finished two-room home. The first major municipal project began in Huauchinango, Puebla, where the local government hired EcoDom to provide panels for 500 room extensions. Each extension covered about 135 square feet. After that project, officials in Chiconcuautla hired the company to build 150 separate homes measuring 460 square feet each. A second agreement of the same size was later signed with authorities in Pahuatlán for another 150 homes. The company’s work has also created a new supply chain that is changing how informal waste collectors earn money in the region.Informal waste collectors in Mexico have traditionally received very little money from commercial recycling companies. Some earn as little as 1.5 pesos, or six cents, for every kilogram of plastic they collect. To maintain a reliable supply of plastic for its factory, EcoDom created buying agreements that pay local collectors much more. By offering better prices per kilogram, the company has nearly doubled the earnings of some independent waste collectors in the region. The system also helps provide the factory with its daily supply of five and a half tonnes of plastic, keeping the material out of landfills and waterways. According to information cited by Unreasonable Group, less than five per cent of plastic made worldwide is recovered or kept out of landfills. Between 10 million and 20 million tonnes of plastic enter the oceans each year, with some types of synthetic material taking up to 1,000 years to break down.After setting up its operations in Puebla, González said he wants to increase factory production, secure larger national contracts and eventually bring the building model to other countries facing similar housing shortages. “This has the potential to grow exponentially,” said González. “The problem of trash is huge in my country. In the whole world, there's a ton of trash. In the next year, I want to grow the company ten-fold. First, we will concentrate in Mexico, but in 3-5 years, we want to go to other countries. There is poverty everywhere. The world is a house for everyone, and it's worth it to fight for expanding this business. I will dedicate the rest of my life to this.” The company’s production records and agreements with local governments show how low-cost recycling technology, combined with public housing support, can turn waste into useful and long-lasting homes for communities.
Article Summary: Mexico is the world’s 12th-largest consumer of plastic and produces more than five million tonnes of plastic waste each year. The World Bank estimates that 11.5 million Mexicans live in extreme poverty on $1.25 or less a day, leaving many people without safe and basic housing. EcoDom, a social enterprise in Puebla state, turns melted plastic waste into strong wall and roofing panels. It supplies building panels directly to local governments and non-governmental organisations.

Article Title: For years, visitors left coins for luck in Giant’s Causeway’s ancient rocks. Years later, more than 10,000 coins have been removed to protect the World Heritage Site
Article Text:
How 10,000 coins began damaging the ancient rocks

More than 20 minutes were needed to free some coins from Giant’s Causeway rocks

The volcanic history behind the Giant’s Causeway’s 40,000 columns

How removal of 10,000 coins could help teach visitors about conservation

For years, visitors to the Giant’s Causeway have left behind more than photographs and memories. Coins were pushed into gaps between the site’s distinctive basalt columns, sometimes as a gesture of luck or affection. What might have seemed harmless began to leave a physical mark on the rocks. As reported by the BBC, conservation work at the Northern Ireland landmark has removed more than 20kg of coins, roughly equivalent to 10,000 pieces. The job was carried out slowly, often one coin at a time, with some proving stubbornly difficult to dislodge. For those doing the work, the task was less about collecting loose change than undoing a practice that had gradually become a problem for the protected landscape. The coins could also introduce metal into a natural environment where conservation teams work to preserve the formations in their original condition. The removal highlights how even small visitor habits can accumulate over time, creating unexpected challenges for protecting one of Northern Ireland’s most famous natural landmarks.The habit of wedging coins into the rocks had existed for years, but the scale of it grew during the past decade.Visitors would press coins into narrow gaps in the columns, with some using other stones to hammer them further into place.The National Trust, which looks after the site, became increasingly concerned about what was happening beneath the surface. A Geological Survey of Northern Ireland report had recommended removing the coins because the metal could affect the rocks both physically and chemically.The problem was not simply the presence of metal. As coins weathered, they could corrode and produce staining on the surrounding basalt. Some had become so tightly lodged that removing them required care to avoid causing further damage."It is a relief, the coins were doing a significant amount of damage ," Dr Cliff Henry, nature engagement officer with the National Trust.Dr Cliff Henry, a nature engagement officer with the National Trust, said the coins had been capable of putting pressure on the rock around them. As they rusted and expanded, they could press against the sides of the gaps and the columns above.The marks left behind were visible too. Rust-coloured staining had spread down sections of the dark rock, making some areas look markedly different from the natural basalt around them. Visitors also risked widening natural cracks when forcing coins into them, especially when stones were used to hammer the metal deeper. Over time, repeated pressure could weaken fragile edges and leave small chips, turning a seemingly harmless souvenir tradition into a growing threat to the protected geological formation.The removal work began in May last year and eventually became a slow exercise in patience. Specialist stonemason Nathan Morrow was brought in to deal with the coins. The work was described as both satisfying and frustrating because there was no single method that worked every time.Coins close to the edge of a rock could sometimes be gripped with pliers. Others were buried deeper in narrow spaces and required a grouting tool to loosen them.A particularly stubborn coin could take more than 20 minutes to remove. Others came away almost immediately.For those firmly wedged in place, Morrow found that repeatedly working a coin backwards and forwards could gradually free it. The aim was to get it moving without putting unnecessary pressure on the surrounding stone.It was painstaking work, and the final haul illustrates just how widespread the practice had become. More than 20kg of unwanted coins have now been taken from the site.The Giant’s Causeway itself was not shaped by people, of course. Its roughly 40,000 basalt columns formed through volcanic activity millions of years ago.Molten rock forced its way upwards through cracks in the Earth before cooling. As the lava contracted, it fractured into the striking geometric columns that now extend towards the sea.Their unusual appearance has long attracted explanations beyond geology. Irish legend tells of the giant Finn McCool, or Fionn mac Cumhaill, who supposedly built the causeway as a route to Scotland so he could confront another giant.Another story links Finn to the Isle of Man, said to have been formed when he threw a piece of earth during a fight and missed his target.The coin problem is a reminder that even seemingly minor visitor behaviour can accumulate at a heavily visited natural site. Hundreds of thousands of people come to the Giant’s Causeway each year, and a gesture that takes only a few seconds can be repeated thousands of times.For the National Trust, removing the coins is only part of the job. New signs have been installed asking visitors not to put coins into the rocks, while the organisation has also been using its social media channels to reinforce the message.Dr Henry has suggested that visitors who want to leave money behind should instead use a charity collection box, where it can be put to practical use.
Article Summary: Coins were pushed into gaps between the site’s distinctive basalt columns, sometimes as a gesture of luck or affection. What might have seemed harmless began to leave a physical mark on the rocks. More than 20kg of unwanted coins have now been taken from the site.

Article Title: A New Mexico carver, Ross Ward, spent decades building Tinkertown from carved wood and 50,000 discarded bottles; the 22-room museum opened to visitors in 1983
Article Text:
Ross Ward spent 40 years hand-building Tinkertown from carved wood. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

From carnival signs to tiny towns

A museum built one piece at a time

Hundreds of tiny toy dolls and other figures fill the rooms and balconies (and even the roof!) of miniature buildings on display at Tinkertown Museum on the Turquoise Trail in New Mexico. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Keeping Ward's world alive

A childhood fascination with miniature figures eventually became one of New Mexico's most unusual folk-art attractions. In 1962, self-taught artist Ross Ward began carving small wooden figures as a hobby, initially creating scenes that could travel with him to fairs and carnivals. Over the next four decades, the hobby expanded into an elaborate handmade world at Sandia Park, where thousands of carved characters, animated displays, collections of Americana and walls made from tens of thousands of discarded glass bottles eventually became Tinkertown Museum.According to Spaces Archives , Ward was born in 1940 and developed his artistic skills without formal training. After working in roadside attractions, he spent years travelling with carnivals and circuses, painting banners and advertisements. At the same time, he was developing his own miniature figures. His carvings were first displayed as a travelling exhibit at county fairs and carnivals during the 1960s and 1970s, giving him a way to take his growing collection on the road. As the collection expanded, however, Ward began looking beyond the limitations of a portable display. After settling in New Mexico, he started building permanent settings for his figures, gradually transforming the travelling collection into a larger, interconnected environment.The figures were no longer simply individual carvings. He created a Western town, shops, a saloon, a hotel, a blacksmith and other scenes populated by tiny wooden inhabitants. The displays were designed to move as well as to be viewed, turning the miniature town into a kind of mechanical theatre. Visitors could also activate some of the scenes with coins, setting figures and machines into motion.The museum itself eventually became another part of Ward’s art. More than 50,000 glass bottles were incorporated into concrete walls around the building, many of them collected from roadsides, dumps and neighbours. What began as a practical use for discarded bottles developed into an architectural feature that gave Tinkertown its distinctive appearance. Ward also filled the site with discarded objects that might otherwise have been thrown away. Wagon wheels, old signs, tools, toys, agricultural equipment and other pieces of Americana became part of the surroundings. Over time, the portable miniature displays and the permanent architecture became increasingly interconnected, making the building itself part of the experience. The result was less like a conventional museum and more like a maze in which the building, collections and sculptures formed a single artwork.According to Tinkertown Museum , the museum opened to the public in 1983 and had grown from Ross Ward’s small summer cabin into a 22-room collection of handmade displays. Its winding spaces contained an animated miniature Western town, a detailed circus, coin-operated attractions such as Otto the One-Man-Band, collections of antique tools and dolls, thousands of wedding-cake figures and the 35-foot antique sailboat Theodora R. By then, what had begun as a travelling collection had become a permanent environment that combined Ward’s carving, mechanical work, collecting and construction. He spent much of his adult life carving, painting, collecting and constructing, rather than producing a single finished work for a gallery. The museum therefore became as much a record of his interests as a display of his craftsmanship. His attraction to the Old West, travelling shows and everyday American life was reflected repeatedly in both the carved scenes and the objects surrounding them. The building’s handmade character also placed Tinkertown within the tradition of self-taught and outsider folk-art environments, where artists transformed private properties into immersive spaces rather than creating isolated artworks.The Spaces archive also notes that Ward continued developing Tinkertown for decades, but his health eventually limited his work. He was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease in 1998 and died in 2002, leaving behind the museum he had spent much of his life constructing. His wife, Carla, and other family members continued caring for the attraction and keeping it open to visitors. According to the museum, the attraction grew from welcoming 943 visitors in 1983 to attracting around 25,000 visitors each season. In 2026, the family converted the museum into a public nonprofit, a step intended to support the long-term preservation of its buildings, artwork and Ward’s wider artistic legacy. More than six decades after Ward began carving his miniature figures, Tinkertown remains a testament to what can emerge from a lifelong hobby. Its maze of handmade scenes, collections and bottle walls preserves not only Ward’s craftsmanship but also his vision of creating an environment entirely on his own terms.
Article Summary: Self-taught artist Ross Ward spent 40 years hand-building Tinkertown in New Mexico. The museum opened to the public in 1983 and had grown from a small summer cabin. It contained an animated miniature Western town, a detailed circus, coin-operated attractions such as Otto the One-Man-Band.

Article Title: In 1948, retired Wisconsin lumberjack Fred Smith began shaping a concrete park by hand; by 1964, he had created 237 sculptures beside Highway 13
Article Text:
In 1948, retired Wisconsin lumberjack Fred Smith began shaping a concrete park by hand. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

From lumber camps to concrete

A roadside panorama of America

"Mr Knox and Oxen" is a sculpture by Fred Smith, a lumberjack, barkeeper, and self-taught artist. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

From roadside curiosity to preserved landmark

A retired lumberjack in northern Wisconsin once turned his own property into an unlikely outdoor museum, filling it with towering concrete figures, animals, local characters and scenes from American history. What began in 1948, when Fred Smith stopped working in the logging camps, grew over the next 16 years into Wisconsin Concrete Park, a sprawling collection of 237 sculptures beside Highway 13 near Phillips.According to Wisconsin Concrete Park , Smith was born in 1886 to German immigrant parents in Price County and spent much of his working life in the Northwoods lumber camps. He also farmed, grew ginseng and Christmas trees, and in 1936 opened the Rock Garden Tavern on his homestead. The tavern later became an important source of material for his sculptures, particularly the discarded beer bottles whose glass he embedded in the concrete. When Smith left the logging camps in 1948, retirement did not mean slowing down. He began with relatively modest bas-relief plaques and gradually moved towards larger, three-dimensional figures. His early subjects included local people and events, but his imagination soon expanded.There were lumberjacks and Native American figures, pioneers and politicians, animals, biblical subjects and characters drawn from popular legends.Smith's first creations were closely connected to the place where he lived. Rather than making sculptures for galleries or exhibitions, he incorporated them into the landscape around his home, tavern and rock garden. The result was not a conventional sculpture garden with works displayed separately. The figures occupied the same landscape, which Smith called his "Wisconsin Concrete Park". The National Register of Historic Places later described it as a cohesive built environment combining local and national history with Smith's own artistic vision.His materials were as unconventional as his subjects. Smith built wooden frameworks, wrapped them with wire and added layers of hand-mixed cement. Broken bottles, pieces of glass, mirrors, stones and other found objects were pressed into the surfaces. For larger sculptures, he often constructed components separately before assembling them at their final locations. The method was practical and gave the figures their distinctive rough, textured appearance.Smithsonian Magazine notes that Smith's sculptures became a kind of three-dimensional scrapbook. Paul Bunyan, the legendary giant lumberjack associated with the Northwoods, stands among figures representing people and stories from much wider American culture. There are sculptures of Abraham and Mary Todd Lincoln, Sacagawea and the Statue of Liberty, alongside animals and scenes inspired by everyday rural life. One of the park's most unusual works depicts an enormous muskellunge being pulled by horses. Smith deliberately blended local history with national history, folklore and legend. His sculptures placed regional characters alongside famous historical figures, while animals and mythical subjects appeared within the same landscape. The result was a richly varied environment where different parts of Smith’s imagination and the history of the Northwoods existed side by side.According to Conservation Online , Fred Smith’s Wisconsin Concrete Park belongs to a wider tradition of outdoor environments created by self-taught artists, combining materials such as concrete, wood, glass, metal and stone. The scale and subject matter of Smith’s work were closely tied to his life in Wisconsin’s Northwoods and his years as a lumberjack. Even as arthritis made the physical work more difficult, he continued creating and installing sculptures with help from family and neighbours. Smith’s sculpting career came to an end in 1964 after he suffered a stroke.Wisconsin Concrete Park also notes that Smith died in 1976, but his unusual landscape survived him. Shortly afterwards, the Kohler Foundation acquired the property and began restoration work. The timing proved unfortunate: a powerful windstorm struck the area in 1977, damaging many sculptures and uprooting trees across the site. Restoration nevertheless continued, and the property was eventually transferred to Price County. A second major storm in 1987 reinforced the need for long-term stewardship and regular maintenance rather than one-time repairs.That need for continued care remains relevant because Smith's sculptures were designed for outdoor display and contain materials that deteriorate differently. Wooden internal supports can decay, metal armatures can corrode and repeated freezing and thawing can crack concrete. Glass and other decorative pieces can also loosen. Conservators therefore carry out ongoing work to reinforce structures, repair cracks, stabilise foundations and replace damaged internal components while trying to retain Smith's original appearance. According to the Wisconsin Historical Society , the park was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2005, recognising not just the individual sculptures but the entire environment Smith created. Today, the roadside landscape south of Phillips remains home to his collection, with the sculptures spread across the property among trees and pathways. What began with a retired lumberjack pouring concrete on his homestead has outlasted the man who made it. He kept making sculptures until his property became a record of the people, stories and landscapes that filled his imagination.
Article Summary: In 1948, retired Wisconsin lumberjack Fred Smith began shaping a concrete park by hand. Smith built wooden frameworks, wrapped them with wire and added layers of hand-mixed cement. Broken bottles, pieces of glass, mirrors, stones and other found objects were pressed into the surfaces.

Article Title: In 1994, Arthur and Helen Chapman bought a former Black schoolhouse in Maryland; today, its original blackboard remains
Article Text:
AI REPRESENTATION: One of the classrooms still contains the original blackboard used by students at the school even after two decades | ChatGPT

AI REPRESENTATION: One of the classrooms still contains the original blackboard used by students at the school even after two decades | ChatGPT

A two-room school for Black children

High school was not an option nearby

The Chapmans bought the abandoned schoolhouse

The original classroom is still there

Brown v. Board of Education

Lutherville Colored School, early 1900s | Facebook/Baltimore Past and Present Photos

A schoolhouse that became a museum

Arthur and Helen Chapman bought Lutherville Colored School No. 24 in Maryland in 1994, when the former two-room schoolhouse had already spent decades out of use. They restored the building and turned it into a museum of African American history. One of the classrooms still contains the original blackboard used by students at the school even after two decades.The schoolhouse was constructed around 1908 and opened in 1909 on School Lane in Lutherville, Baltimore County. It was built for Black children during the era of segregated public education and served students in grades one through seven. The building had two classrooms. The first three grades occupied one room, while grades four through seven used the larger room. Students came from Lutherville and nearby communities including Cockeysville, Beaver Dam, Riderwood, Ruxton, Brightside and Bare Hills.The school did not have indoor bathrooms, so students and teachers used an outhouse. Teaching materials were also limited compared with those available at white schools in the county, according to Baltimore Heritage’s historical account For Black students who wanted to continue their education beyond the elementary grades, opportunities were restricted. Baltimore County did not have a public high school for Black students until Carver High School opened in Towson in 1939. Before that, some students had to attend schools in Baltimore City. For families who could not afford transportation or other costs, continuing their education could be difficult. Lutherville Colored School No. 24 eventually closed in 1955, and the building was later used by Baltimore County for storage.Arthur and Helen Chapman purchased the former school from Baltimore County in 1994. The couple had a family connection to the building through Marie E. Jackson, a former student who had lived across the street. The Chapmans spent more than $100,000 restoring the structure, according to the museum’s own account . They dedicated it as a museum in 1996 in Jackson’s honor.The restoration preserved the building as a schoolhouse rather than turning it into a conventional private residence or commercial property. The museum’s collection includes schoolbooks, report cards, oil lamps, furniture and oral histories connected to the school and the surrounding Black community.The original blackboard and cement foundation survived, and one classroom has been arranged to show how the school looked during its operating years. The Associated Press documented the preserved blackboard when it reported on Maryland’s former segregated schools. Books, desks and other classroom materials are displayed alongside information about the students who attended.The preservation also keeps the school’s place in Baltimore County’s segregated education system visible. Afterin 1954, Maryland’s segregated school system began moving toward integration, and Lutherville Colored School No. 24 closed the following year.The museum has remained connected to the community more than a century after the school opened. Former students and their families have returned for gatherings, while the building has been used to preserve photographs, documents and memories associated with the school. Arthur and Helen Chapman died in 2021. Their son, David Chapman, later took over ownership, while Karen Darden has helped operate the museum and organize events. The former Lutherville Colored School No. 24 remains at its original location, with its classroom and blackboard preserved as part of the museum.
Article Summary: Arthur and Helen Chapman bought Lutherville Colored School No. 24 in Maryland in 1994. They restored the building and turned it into a museum of African American history. One of the classrooms still contains the original blackboard used by students at the school even after two decades.
