Danny Boy O’Connor first saw the Tulsa house being used as the Curtis brothers’ home inwhen he was touring the city with House of Pain in 2009. The 1920s bungalow at 731 North St. Louis Avenue was still standing, but it was badly deteriorated. Years later, O’Connor bought the property and decided not to repair it as a private home; he wanted to turn it into a museum devoted to S.E. Hinton’s novel and Francis Ford Coppola ’s 1983 film. Smithsonian reports that O’Connor bought the house in 2015, while the museum’s own account and a 2016 fundraiser describe the purchase as taking place in 2016.Smithsonian describes the one-story Craftsman bungalow as being in terrible condition when he eventually bought it. O’Connor estimated that simply making the property livable would require about $150,000. Instead of stopping at a basic renovation, he planned to restore the house to resemble its appearance in the movie and fill it with material connected to. The project would eventually require more time and money than he had expected.A contemporary report from Tulsa television station KJRH said O’Connor planned to reproduce the living room and dining room from the film, down to details including the couch, green curtains, fish bowl and pencil sharpeners.In 2009, while in Tulsa with House of Pain, O’Connor paid a cab driver $100 to take him around the city looking for locations from. He found the Curtis brothers’ house and was struck by how poorly it had been maintained.The discovery also led him to establish the Delta Bravo Urban Exploration Team, a group that documented locations associated with movies and other pieces of popular culture.O’Connor had grown up with a difficult family life and later struggled with alcohol and drugs. In thestory, he identified with the Curtis brothers and their experiences of family, hardship and loyalty. By the time the property went up for sale, O’Connor had decided that he wanted to save it. Smithsonian reported that he had little memorabilia from the movie at the time, just a poster, but still chose to turn the house into a museum.Before moving ahead with the museum, O’Connor contacted S.E. Hinton, who wrotewhile she was a teenager in Tulsa. Hinton agreed to support the project and contributed $10,000, according to Smithsonian. She also gave O’Connor a brown leather jacket worn in the film by Matt Dillon and C. Thomas Howell.The restoration was initially expected to take about six months. Instead, it stretched beyond three years and ultimately cost about $175,000, according to Smithsonian. The early fundraising effort shows how different the final project was from the original plan. A 2016 GoFundMe campaign launched by O’Connor described the property as being in extremely poor condition and sought money to restore it to its movie appearance. The campaign said the goal was to open the house to the public as a museum containing O’Connor’s collection ofmemorabilia.The restoration was based on the 1983 movie rather than simply recreating a generic 1920s Tulsa home, and the museum’s collection eventually grew to include movie costumes, furniture, photographs, paintings, foreign editions of the book and other memorabilia. Smithsonian reported that the roughly 1,400-square-foot interior includes Ponyboy’s desk, wardrobe pieces and props associated with the film. The house itself remains recognizable from the film. The museum describes its purpose as preserving both the home and memorabilia from, which was filmed in Tulsa in 1982.O’Connor’s six-month estimate turned into a restoration lasting more than three years, and the Outsiders House Museum officially opened in August 2019. By then, the restored house had become a public museum rather than simply a preserved movie location. Smithsonian reported that about 20,000 people visited in 2022, with school groups visiting during the week and the general public attending on weekends. The museum remains at 731 North St. Louis Avenue in Tulsa, and its current site lists weekend public hours and describes the property as dedicated to preserving the house and memorabilia from the film.

The 1920s bungalow at 731 North St. Louis Avenue was still standing, but it was badly deteriorated. O'Connor bought the property and decided not to repair it as a private home; he wanted to turn it into a museum devoted to S.E. Hinton’s novel and Francis Ford Coppola ’s 1983 film.

Article Title: In 1881, Judge Owen Denny shipped 60 Chinese pheasants to America because he liked their meat; the survivors helped establish a wild population in Oregon
Article Text:
The pheasants left China aboard the Otago, a ship that reached Port Townsend on March 13, 1881 | Wikimedia Commons​

The pheasants left China aboard the Otago, a ship that reached Port Townsend on March 13, 1881 | Wikimedia Commons​

Denny first encountered the birds in China

The first shipment went badly

Otago

The 1882 release established the Oregon population

The birds multiplied quickly

Female pheasant | Wikimedia Commons

From Oregon to other states

Judge Owen Nickerson Denny wanted Chinese pheasants in Oregon partly because he liked eating them. In 1881, while serving as the United States consul general in Shanghai, he arranged for about 60 ring-necked pheasants to be shipped from China to Washington state. Most survived the ocean voyage, but the difficult journey from Port Townsend to Oregon killed many of them. The few that remained were released along the lower Columbia River. Denny sent more birds the following year, and the 1882 release in Oregon’s Willamette Valley became the first successful introduction of ring-necked pheasants in the United States, according to the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife Denny was an Oregon native who had entered the diplomatic service and was serving in China when he became interested in the pheasants living around Shanghai. The birds were already being trapped by Chinese farmers and sold as food. Historical accounts record that Denny considered the birds good eating and wanted to see them established in Oregon. He eventually arranged to have them captured and transported across the Pacific along with other Chinese birds and plants. HistoryLink, a Washington historical organization , records Denny’s own explanation of the decision. He wrote that the pheasants were delicious and that he imagined what it would be like to release them in Oregon.The pheasants left China aboard the, a ship that reached Port Townsend on March 13, 1881. Most of the birds survived the ocean crossing. The birds had to be transported from Port Townsend to Portland, and the unfamiliar movement of trains and boats caused them to panic. According to a historical account compiled by HistoryLink, the pheasants beat themselves against the bars of their cages during the journey. Only a small number survived the trip to Oregon, which were released on the lower Columbia River near Portland, but historians have disagreed about how successfully this first group established itself. Some later accounts credited the surviving birds with reproducing, while others considered the first attempt unsuccessful.Denny arranged another shipment in 1882, this time sending ring-necked pheasants directly toward Oregon. The birds were released in the Willamette Valley, where farmland, grain and vegetation provided suitable habitat. The Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife identifies that 1882 release as the first successful introduction of ring-necked pheasants in the United States. The birds adapted to the agricultural landscape and their numbers grew rapidly. Denny made another shipment in 1884, with additional birds released on Protection Island near Port Townsend. The pheasants continued to spread through Oregon and Washington.HistoryLink records that ring-necked pheasants had spread through Oregon and Washington by the late 19th century. Oregon eventually opened its first pheasant hunting season in 1892, and reports from the period said hunters killed about 50,000 birds on the first day. The birds were initially known in Oregon as China pheasants or Denny pheasants. Their descendants spread beyond the original release sites, through the help of further introductions and transfers to other parts of the country. The Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife describes the Willamette Valley as the site of the first successful U.S. introduction and notes that the birds soon expanded into the tens of thousands.The success of the Pacific Northwest population encouraged people elsewhere in the United States to introduce pheasants for hunting. The ring-necked pheasant is native to Asia, not North America. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration notes that after Denny’s introduction, ring-necked pheasants were released in practically every U.S. state.Not every American pheasant population can be traced directly to Denny’s original birds, however. Later introductions involved other pheasant stocks and releases by game farms and private organizations. Still, the Oregon population became the model for establishing the species in the wild in the United States. Oregon wildlife officials describe ring-necked pheasants as farmland birds that depend heavily on cereal grains and other seeds, with taller vegetation providing cover.
Article Summary: U.S. consul general Owen Nickerson Denny wanted Chinese pheasants in Oregon partly because he liked eating them. In 1881, he arranged for about 60 ring- necked p heasants to be shipped from China to Washington state. Most survived the ocean voyage, but the difficult journey from Port Townsend to Oregon killed many of them. Denny sent more birds the following year, and the 1882 release in Oregon’s Willamette Valley became the first successful introduction.

Article Title: USS Abraham Lincoln sails past Singapore on way home after gruelling Middle East deployment
Article Text:
USS Abraham Lincoln has been at centre of controversy over its prolonged deployment and is now headed home

Poll Vote & Share your view How concerned are you about the mental health of servicemen after prolonged deployments? Very concerned Somewhat concerned Not concerned at all 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

US aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln sailed past Singapore early Sunday as it headed home after an extended deployment in the Middle East, with the warship expected to make a port visit in Thailand for rest and recovery.Indonesia’s Batam island, across the Singapore Strait, spotted the massive carrier transiting waters near Singapore shortly after 1 am local tim, as reported by AP.The Lincoln, one of the US Navy’s largest warships, had spent months supporting American combat operations in the Middle East war against Iran. Its deployment lasted more than 250 days, including more than 200 days without a port call; a period described as a modern-day record.However, the prolonged deployment has drawn scrutiny over conditions aboard the carrier, which has about 5,000 sailors and Marines. Military outlets and other reports have cited declining morale, mental-health concerns, intermittent shortages of food and hygiene supplies, and problems with toilets and water systems.Local media reports have also described suicide attempts and sailors going overboard during the deployment.Although the US Navy has disputed claims of a broader mental-health crisis, saying it had not observed an increase in suicidal thoughts or attempts aboard the ship and that medical, religious and mental-health professionals were available to the crew.US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had also said reports about conditions aboard the Lincoln were “completely misrepresented”. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao also defended the crew’s performance earlier this month, saying the sailors had been pushed to their limits but continued to meet the demands of the mission.Cao said the Lincoln spent 266 days deployed, including 200 days in a combat zone, while its strike group conducted more than 10,000 sorties and dropped about 1.5 million pounds of ordnance.The carrier is now returning to its US base as part of a planned rotation. Thai officials have said it will stop in Thailand before continuing its journey home.
Article Summary: US aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln sailed past Singapore early Sunday as it headed home after an extended deployment in the Middle East. The warship is expected to make a port visit in Thailand for rest and recovery. The prolonged deployment has drawn scrutiny over conditions aboard the carrier, which has about 5,000 sailors and Marines.

Article Title: A 55-year-old Missouri official reached the 13,804-foot summit of Wyoming's highest mountain and signed its register; he then disappeared for 5 days before rescuers found him alive and severely dehydr
Article Text:
A 55-year-old Missouri official reached the 13,804-foot summit of Wyoming's highest mountain and signed its register

A difficult climb to the summit

Search teams mobilise

Rescue and recovery in Pinedale

The dangers of Gannett Peak

Poll Vote & Share your view Would you consider undertaking a challenging peak like Gannett Peak? Absolutely, I love a challenge! Probably not, too risky for me 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

55-year-old Missouri deputy attorney general who had been missing in Wyoming's rugged Wind River Range for five days has been rescued alive, shortly after search crews confirmed that he had reached the 13,804-foot summit of Gannett Peak. Shaun Mackelprang was found on Wednesday morning, 26 August, walking in a confused state and severely dehydrated near Scott Lake, about eight and a half miles from the nearest trailhead. Searchers from Sublette County Search and Rescue and Tip Top Search and Rescue gave him intravenous fluids at the scene before flying him by helicopter to a medical facility in Pinedale. The rescue brought an end to a multi-day search across one of the most remote mountain wilderness areas in the United States. The operation began after Mackelprang failed to return from a solo trip to climb Wyoming's highest mountain.According to Wyoming news outlet Cowboy State Daily, Mackelprang made the trip as part of his goal to climb the highest natural point in all 50 US states. Gannett Peak was the 45th summit on his list. He left on Thursday, 20 August, from the Green River Lakes Trailhead. He set up a campsite in the backcountry before making his final climb towards the summit on Friday, 21 August.Reaching Gannett Peak requires a difficult 35-to-50-mile round trip through rough terrain, including large boulder fields, steep snow slopes and fast-changing mountain weather. Mackelprang reached the 13,804-foot summit on Friday and signed the official peak register, a logbook kept in a protected container at the top. However, strong thunderstorms and quickly changing weather moved through the range during his descent. He became lost in the difficult alpine terrain.When Mackelprang failed to return as planned over the weekend, his family became worried. His sister Sheila contacted authorities in Wyoming on Sunday, 23 August, starting the emergency search. Deputies from the Sublette County Sheriff's Office found Mackelprang's vehicle parked at the Green River Lakes Trailhead. This confirmed that he was still somewhere in the backcountry. The search soon expanded, bringing in ground teams, aerial drone crews and a specialised helicopter team from Tip Top Search and Rescue, a non-profit volunteer group based in western Wyoming. A major breakthrough came when other climbers who had reached Gannett Peak after Mackelprang provided photographs of the peak register. The photos showed that he had reached the summit before disappearing. This helped search coordinators focus on the area between the summit and his campsite. Sublette County Sheriff's Office spokesman Travis Bingham told Cowboy State Daily that ground crews searched different grid sections using information from hikers and other physical clues. “It was a ground team that was just clearing an area and came upon him,” Bingham told Cowboy State Daily. “There's not really one smoking gun thing that pointed us there. You just follow the clues.” Mackelprang's brother, Romel, said the climber may have become confused after walking towards another lake that looked similar to the one where he had originally camped. “They found him wandering at a lake that probably looks similar to the one that his tent was pitched at,” Romel Mackelprang told Cowboy State Daily shortly after learning he had been found. “We don't know.”Despite spending five days exposed to high-altitude conditions with very little water, Mackelprang was still able to stand and walk when ground teams found him at about 9:45 a.m. on Wednesday. He was flown to St. John's Health clinical facilities in Pinedale, where doctors treated him for severe dehydration, exhaustion, bruising and widespread skin injuries. By Thursday, 27 August, his family said his condition had improved significantly. From his hospital room in Pinedale, Mackelprang thanked the search teams who put themselves at risk to find him in statements published by Cowboy State Daily. He gave special thanks to Tip Top Search and Rescue and the Sublette County Sheriff's Office for being “ready and prepared to stand up for me in my time of need.” “It's no easy task to put your life on the line for someone else, especially a stranger who has no place in their lives,” Mackelprang said. “These women and men did so without a second thought. May God bless them for their good deeds and compassion.” Officials in Missouri also praised the search effort. Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway released a statement thanking the agencies involved in bringing her colleague home safely. “We are thrilled to hear that Deputy Attorney General Shaun Mackelprang has been located,” Hanaway said in a statement released to media organisations. “Our office is beyond grateful for everyone's prayers and the steadfast work of the Sublette County Sheriff's Office and drone team, Tip Top Search and Rescue's volunteers and helicopter crew, and Wyoming State leaders.”Mountaineering experts consider Gannett Peak, along with Montana's Granite Peak, one of the hardest state highpoints to climb in the contiguous United States. Unlike mountains that can be reached by roads or short maintained trails, Gannett Peak requires a multi-day wilderness trip just to reach the base of the summit. Climbers must deal with loose rock and scree, hidden crevasses and sudden cold weather that can send temperatures below freezing even in late August. Mackelprang has worked in the Missouri Attorney General's Office since May 2021. He previously handled high-profile state legal cases before the Missouri Supreme Court. He remains in Pinedale recovering, while his family prepares for his eventual discharge and return to Missouri.
Article Summary: Missouri deputy attorney general Shaun Mackelprang, 55, had been missing in Wyoming's rugged Wind River Range for five days. Search crews confirmed that he had reached the 13,804-foot summit of Gannett Peak. He was found walking in a confused state and severely dehydrated near Scott Lake, about eight and a half miles from the nearest trailhead.

Article Title: Teenager accused of killing mother and brother allegedly used ChatGPT to create stories about murdering his family: What prosecutors found online before the double homicide
Article Text:
Prosecutors said the teenager used ChatGPT to develop fictional stories involving family killings.

A welfare check that uncovered a family tragedy

What prosecutors say about ChatGPT

Father had reportedly become concerned

What charges does Arjun face?

A case that raises difficult questions about AI

There was nothing unusual about the way the tragedy first came to light. A tutor arrived at a family home in Acton, Massachusetts, for an appointment. No one answered the door. The father could not reach his wife or children either. He called the police and asked them to check on his family.What officers found inside the house on Tuesday, August 11, turned a routine welfare check into a double-homicide investigation. The bodies of 45-year-old Sudha Venkatesan and her 14-year-old son, Siddharth Aravind, were found inside the home on August 11. Their 17-year-old son, Arjun Aravind, was missing. Within hours, police found him in his mother's car in nearby Wayland and arrested him.Now, the case has drawn attention far beyond the Massachusetts town because prosecutors say the teenager had recently been using the internet- including AI and ChatGPT- to search for and create “fictional scenarios” involving the killing of his own family.According to CNN, prosecutors said Arjun had used the AI chatbot to explore what they described as “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” about killing his family.Middlesex County District Attorney Marian Ryan said investigators found that he had been creating Gothic-novel-style stories, developing characters and asking questions that appeared to relate to threats against his family.The sequence of events began when a tutor arrived at the family's Martha Lane home and could not get inside. Arjun's father, who had been unable to contact his family, then contacted Acton police. Officers who went to the house found Siddharth on the first floor and his mother in the basement, according to prosecutors. Both had suffered obvious trauma.At a subsequent court hearing, prosecutors described evidence of a physical and violent struggle and said blunt-force trauma had been involved. The official cause and manner of death were initially awaiting findings from the medical examiner. Arjun was not at the house. Investigators said he had left in his mother's Honda Accord.The search ended early the following morning when Wayland police responding to an unrelated alarm spotted the vehicle in a parking lot. Arjun was inside and was arrested without incident, authorities said. Items found in the car were also said to correspond with the murder scene.The most unusual detail in the investigation emerged after Arjun's arrest. Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan said the teenager had recently displayed what investigators considered concerning behaviour. This included internet activity and use of ChatGPT to explore “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” concerning the killing of his family.Ryan said the teenager appeared to be using the chatbot to develop fictional narratives, including Gothic-style stories and characters. Investigators believed some of those scenarios appeared connected to threats against members of his family.The detail has inevitably raised questions about the role of artificial intelligence in the case. But prosecutors have not said that ChatGPT instructed Arjun to commit the killings, nor have authorities established that the chatbot caused the alleged violence.That distinction is important. The investigation is examining Arjun's internet activity as part of a much larger picture of his behaviour and circumstances.Court proceedings have also shed light on concerns within the family before the killings. According to CBS News Boston, Arjun's father had become worried about his son's behaviour and internet activity and had begun hiding knives in the house. The precise reasons for those concerns, and whether they were directly connected to the alleged killings, remain part of the investigation.Arjun's defence lawyer, Debra DeWitt, has requested a psychiatric evaluation. She told reporters after his arraignment that the family had recently moved to Acton partly to provide a support system and schooling for the children.The teenager has pleaded not guilty.Arjun has been charged with two counts of murder, along with charges including assault and battery on a family or household member, assault and battery and offences related to the alleged unauthorised use and theft of a motor vehicle. He was held without bail following his arraignment. His next major court appearance, a probable-cause hearing, is scheduled for September 11.The case remains under investigation, and the allegations against Arjun have not been proven in court.The Massachusetts case is likely to fuel an already growing debate over how generative AI interacts with vulnerable or troubled users, particularly children and teenagers.But the facts available so far point to a more complicated question than whether an AI chatbot is responsible for a crime. Here, prosecutors say they discovered disturbing AI-assisted fantasies alongside other concerning behaviour. What remains unclear is how those thoughts developed, what role, if any, the technology played in the teenager's actions, and whether warning signs could have been recognised earlier.For now, the central facts remain stark: two members of an Indian-origin family in Massachusetts are dead, a 17-year-old family member has been charged with their killings, and investigators are continuing to piece together what happened inside the Acton home.
Article Summary: Arjun Aravind, 17, charged with two counts of murder, along with assault and battery. Bodies of Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and her 14-year-old son, Siddharth, were found inside the home on August 11. Within hours, police found him in his mother's car in nearby Wayland and arrested him. Prosecutors said Arjun had used the AI chatbot to explore what they described as ‘theoretical ideas or fantasy stories’ about killing his family.

Article Title: A Milwaukee landlord found a peculiar print hanging in a vacant apartment; it turned out to be an original Picasso that had been missing for eight years
Article Text: When an original Picasso disappeared from a Milwaukee gallery in 2018, owners wondered if they would ever see it again. But in August 2026, a man turned the art over to the police. Timothy Dertz noticed an intriguing artwork on the wall of his apartment after his tenant moved out. When he asked an antique dealer to take a look, the two men noticed a signature in green crayon: 'Picasso', reported Smithsonian Magazine.The artwork was a print of a bullfighter and a thick layer of dust had collected on the top of the frame. The landlord figured that the print must have been hanging in that spot for some time. “It was in a back bedroom behind a door,” Dertz told WISN-TV’s Stephen Cohn. “A very odd placement for such a piece of art.”When the two dug deeper, they realised that the artwork was a 1949 Pablo Picasso etching called Torero, Spanish for 'bullfighter'. It had been missing from Milwaukee's DeLind Fine Art Appraisals since February 2018. At the time of its disappearance, it was valued at $35,000 to $50,000.The “Torero” print, one of 30 of its kind, was originally commissioned for sale at a gallery owned by Bill DeLind, who told The Associated Press Friday that when police called him to let him know it had been found, “I was overwhelmed.I was at a loss for words. It was an overwhelming moment for me.”The disappearance was distressing for the owners of the gallery, a small operation with no working security cameras at the time of the theft. On February 16, 2018, “somebody walked in in the middle of the day and picked a Picasso off the wall and walked out with it,” DeLind tells the Associated Press’ Scott Bauer. “Nobody noticed—not me, not my partner.” DeLind had seen the etching hanging on the wall that very morning. His business partner, Michael Goforth, who died earlier this year, noticed that the artwork wasn’t in its usual spot a few hours later. “I immediately went upstairs,” Goforth told Fox6 News in 2018. “I said, ‘Bill, tell me the Picasso is out on approval.’ And the look he gave me was priceless.”The late co-owner of DeLind’s gallery, Michael Goforth, was deeply invested in trying to recover the print prior to his death earlier this year. DeLind told WITI-TV that Goforth “was so invested in this particular piece. It was an obsession with him that he wanted it back.”The gallery announced a $5,000 reward for the piece’s return a few weeks later. When no new leads materialised, they raised the reward to $7,500 and then $10,000. Every year, on the anniversary of the theft, DeLind and Goforth checked in with the police or contacted local media outlets, hoping to keep the search active.“It was violating,” Goforth told WISN-TV’s Kendall Keys in 2023. “My partner and I have always been open to the public. We’re not stuffy. We like to share these beautiful works of art with everyone in the community. And for someone to just walk in and take advantage of that, it was hurtful.”Robert Wittman, the founder of the FBI’s art crime team, told the TV station that the gallery owners shouldn’t lose hope, as stolen artworks sometimes make their way back. If they come back on the market, somebody usually finds out about their origins. “So if they just sit tight,” he said, “eventually it does show up.”Torero disappeared more than eight years ago, and police told WISN-TV that the statute of limitations for theft and property crimes in Wisconsin is usually six years. Even so, they say that the incident is still under investigation.When Dertz learned of the theft, he became anxious about his unwitting involvement, spending a night pacing and “freaking out,” his girlfriend, Natassha Delgado, as per the Washington Post. Soon, Dertz handed over the artwork to the Milwaukee Police Department on August 5th, 2026.In a statement, the Milwaukee Police Department thanked Dertz, who “recognised the etching print and did the right thing.” Officers contacted Bill DeLind, the art dealer who had co-owned the gallery. He examined the artwork and confirmed that it was the real deal. “I never expected to see it again,” DeLind tells the Washington Post’s Victoria Craw and Grey Battle. “The fact that it would turn up eight years later in perfect condition is just jaw-dropping. ”DeLind said that an insurance company, which paid for the Picasso, is now the piece’s rightful owner. But he’s hopeful that he’ll be allowed to hang Torero in the gallery, even for just a few months, so visitors can see it restored to its former spot on the wall.
Article Summary: A 1949 Pablo Picasso etching called Torero, Spanish for 'bullfighter', was stolen from a Milwaukee gallery in February 2018. The print was valued at $35,000 to $50,000. In August 2026, a man turned the art over to the police.

Article Title: US set to take control of major portion of Venezuelan oil wealth
Article Text:
US set to take control of major portion of Venezuelan oil wealth﻿

Based on a Bloomberg report.

The US is set to take majority control over a huge amount of Venezuela’s oil wealth in an unprecedented manoeuvre that officials said would create the world’s second-largest private oil company by reserves and secure American petroleum supplies for decades to come.President Donald Trump made the announcement about the arrangement in a Truth Social post on Friday night. It represents his latest move to establish US dominance over the Western Hemisphere, countering years of inroads by China, as part of his embrace of the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine.Working with Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, a partnership with private business secured majority US control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves in Venezuela, Trump said.A US official said the country will control 55% of the effective output from the joint venture, and will obtain the oil at cost. The plan represents an unparalleled modern-day intervention into the economy of a South American country Trump once called the 51st US state, harkening back to British control of Iran’s oil fields and the division of Iraqi assets among US and European nations.It marks the culmination of a campaign in which the US captured Venezuela’s president, Nicolas Maduro, in Jan, seized Venezuelan oil tankers and struck several boats allegedly carrying drugs from Venezuela, killing over 200 people.It’s also an untested manoeuvre — one that could be vulnerable to legal challenges and political shifts in Washington. It’s not clear that Trump’s arrangement would be fully embraced by a future American president, or how it might endure any future political upheaval in Venezuela.
Article Summary: President Donald Trump made the announcement about the arrangement in a Truth Social post on Friday night. It represents his latest move to establish US dominance over the Western Hemisphere, countering years of inroads by China. It marks the culmination of a campaign in which the US captured Venezuela’s president, Nicolas Maduro, in Jan.

Article Title: Police officer killed, another wounded in South Carolina park shooting; suspect dead
Article Text:
The shooting unfolded following a call about a domestic dispute

Who was officer Christopher DeLong

Two people, including the suspect, and a police officer were killed, while another officer was wounded in a gunfight at a park in Columbia, South Carolina, the city’s police chief said Saturday (local time).According to police, the incident began around 9:30 a.m. when a woman called authorities to report that a man against whom she had a restraining order was “destroying” property at her home.Officer Christopher DeLong, who was later killed in the exchange of gunfire, arrived at the residence and learned that the suspect had already left. The woman provided DeLong with a description of the man and the vehicle he was believed to be driving.At around 10:30 a.m., DeLong left the residence. Minutes later, after spotting a man near a vehicle matching the description provided by the woman, he radioed in a report of a suspicious person.Officer David Dymock arrived as backup. Minutes later, Dymock radioed other officers saying that both officers “were hit and a suspect was down.”Police identified the suspect as 33-year-old Adam Tyler Dowdy, who they said had a history of arrests in at least four states.Dowdy's previous charges included disorderly conduct, contempt of court, public intoxication, possession of a controlled substance and probation violations.DeLong, 29, had served with the Columbia Police Department for two years before he was killed in the gunfight, Police Chief WH “Skip” Holbrook told reporters at a news conference.He is survived by his wife and their two young children.“Our hearts are broken this evening,” Holbrook remarked, becoming emotional at times. He urged officers to support one another through the tragedy, adding, “We will lean on each other in this tragic time. Let’s pray for this department.”In a social media post, DeLong’s wife described the loss as “living a nightmare” and paid tribute to her husband as the “best dad to our babies.”After the news conference, Holbrook and other law enforcement officials joined a procession from the hospital. Officer Dymock, who was wounded in the shooting, remained in stable condition.The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division would investigate the shooting.
Article Summary: Two people, including the suspect, and a police officer were killed, while another officer was wounded in a gunfight at a park in Columbia, South Carolina. Police identified the suspect as 33-year-old Adam Tyler Dowdy, who they said had a history of arrests in at least four states. The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division would investigate the shooting.

Article Title: Trump-Putin-Zelenskyy summit floated in secret Moscow talks: Report
Article Text:
President Donald Trump waves after arriving off Air Force One, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Md. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

Ratcliffe seeks opening for talks

CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed a trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during his covert trip to Moscow this week, in a bid to revive efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war, Axios reported, citing two people briefed on the matter.Ratcliffe's visit marked his first personal involvement in the Trump administration's diplomatic push to break the deadlock between Russia and Ukraine. He met Russian intelligence chiefs Sergey Naryshkin, head of the SVR foreign intelligence service, and FSB Director Alexander Bortnikov during his trip on Tuesday.According to the sources cited by Axios, Ratcliffe's talks partly focused on whether Russia's intelligence leadership could help persuade Putin to return to US-mediated negotiations with Ukraine.US officials briefed Zelenskyy on Friday about Ratcliffe's discussions in Moscow and the proposal for a three-way summit. The idea has been raised by the Trump administration previously, with Zelenskyy expressing support while Putin has rejected it.Ratcliffe also floated the possibility of restarting peace negotiations, according to the sources. The New York Times separately reported that he gave Bortnikov a bleak assessment of the war and pressed Russia to reach a deal before its position deteriorates further.The Axios sources said Ratcliffe viewed Bortnikov as a constructive interlocutor who could help restart diplomatic efforts. The CIA declined to comment on the discussions.The proposed summit comes as US-mediated negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv remain stalled. Talks were paused in mid-February after the war with Iran began, while White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have separately held discussions with Russian and Ukrainian negotiators in recent months without making significant progress.Ukrainian officials, however, remain deeply sceptical of Putin's intentions. Kyiv has said it has intelligence indicating that Russia could be preparing a major escalation.Zelenskyy's deputy chief of staff, Pavlo Palisa, said on Friday that Putin had ordered the Russian military to prepare several operational scenarios for an offensive in northern Ukraine, including around Kyiv and Chernihiv.At the same time, Zelenskyy's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov said US-mediated talks with Russia could resume in September.Zelenskyy on Friday appeared to welcome Washington's latest diplomatic efforts, thanking the US for what he called the "necessary tone" of its conversations with Russia and saying the Trump administration was advancing a "realistic vision" of what needed to be achieved.
Article Summary: CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Ratcliffe's visit marked his first personal involvement in the Trump administration's diplomatic push to break the deadlock between Russia and Ukraine.

Article Title: Picturesque Danish-style California town, once home to Dolly Parton, faces 31-Airstream resort plan; residents call ‘trailer park’ style ‘completely inappropriate’
Article Text:
Dolly Parton once lived in Solvang, which is now at the centre of a development dispute. (Photo: Getty Images)

‘If it looks like a trailer park ... it’s a trailer park’

Residents question Airstreams and ‘military fortress’ tower

Residents say the proposed Airstream resort does not fit Solvang’s historic Danish-inspired character. (Photo: Getty Images)

Developers agree to go back to the drawing board

Why Solvang is so protective of its character

Locals have criticised the planned lookout tower, with one resident comparing it to an Old West fortress. (Photo: Getty Images)

Another development row at the same site

A plan to transform part of a picturesque California town known for its Danish-inspired architecture and once home to Dolly Parton into an Airstream “glamping” resort has sparked fierce opposition from residents, with one critic branding the proposal a “trailer park” and calling it “completely inappropriate” for the historic community.The proposed development would turn the former Solvang Lumberyard in Solvang, Santa Barbara County, into a resort featuring 31 Airstream units, two hotel suites, a lobby, bar and lounge, a pool, showers, restrooms and a lookout tower.But residents and members of the city's Design Review Committee have questioned whether the development fits the character of the town, particularly because local rules call for architecture reflecting Solvang's historic Spanish Mission-style surroundings.The proposal was discussed by Solvang's Design Review Committee during a pre-application review, where concerns were raised over its design and compatibility with the surrounding area.Dennis Beebe, president of the Santa Ynez Valley Citizens Council, was among the strongest critics of the project.“If it looks like a trailer park and it gleams like a trailer park, in spite of the categorization of a lodging, it’s a trailer park,” Beebe said, as reported by Noozhawk.“I find it completely inappropriate for downtown Solvang.”The proposed development is planned for the 2.19-acre former Solvang Lumberyard property at 1783 and 1793 Mission Drive.While the developers have presented the project as a lodging and glamping destination, critics argue that the collection of shiny aluminum Airstream trailers would clash with Solvang's distinctive architectural identity.The Airstream units were not the only feature to come under scrutiny.Resident Susan Belloni questioned how the proposed accommodation units would relate to the town's Spanish Colonial Revival architecture.“So, I don’t see that 31 mid-century design Chinese aluminum Airstream trailers have anything in common with Spanish colonial revival architecture,” she said, according to Noozhawk.Another concern was the proposed lookout tower, which one resident compared to an “old West military fortress.”Committee member Jennifer Johnson also objected to the concept.“Even if I was going to go camping, which I did all my life growing up, I would never go in an Airstream,” Johnson said.Phil Stevens, who represented the applicant, acknowledged the concerns surrounding the design.Stevens said the project team would develop a new proposal in an attempt to “strike a better balance” between the resort concept and Solvang's architectural character.The project still has to undergo another pre-application review before the developers can move into the development permit process.Solvang is famous for its Danish-inspired buildings, windmills, bakeries, shops and wine tourism and is often described as the “Danish capital of America.”The town's unusual European-style streetscape has helped make it a major tourist attraction in California's Santa Ynez Valley.Dolly Parton also once lived in Solvang, and the small farmhouse associated with her has become a tourist attraction.That tourism appeal is also at the heart of the debate over the proposed Airstream resort. Supporters of new development could argue that additional accommodation would bring more visitors and spending to the town, while opponents fear that developments that do not reflect Solvang's established architecture could ultimately weaken the very identity that draws tourists there.The former lumberyard has been at the centre of development controversy before.In 2022, a proposal for a Mission Hotel and Apartment Project at the site drew opposition from residents concerned about tall buildings and an automated parking structure.Developers subsequently attempted to scale down the project, including reducing the number of parking spaces and the size of the buildings, but it ultimately failed to materialise.The latest proposal has now reopened the debate over what kind of development belongs in the historic tourist town.And with 31 gleaming Airstreams, a pool and a lookout tower planned for the former lumberyard, critics are making it clear they do not want Solvang's Danish charm replaced by what they see as a luxury version of a trailer park.
Article Summary: Solvang, California, is known for its Danish-inspired architecture and was once home to Dolly Parton. The proposed resort would feature 31 Airstream units, two hotel suites, a lobby, bar and lounge, a pool, showers, restrooms and a lookout tower. But residents and members of the city's Design Review Committee have questioned whether the development fits the character of the town.

Article Title: Pakistan hospital fire: 8 officials suspended over deaths of 14 newborns
Article Text: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered the suspension of eight officials and directed that criminal proceedings be initiated against those found responsible for a fire that killed 14 newborns at a hospital in Islamabad, his office said on Saturday.Sharif issued the orders after an interim report by an investigative committee found serious lapses in fire safety and emergency preparedness at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS).The fire broke out on the third-floor nursery on Wednesday, where 15 newborns were being treated. The blaze spread rapidly, and hospital staff were able to rescue only one baby, officials said.The committee found that the nursery had neither a fire alarm nor a sprinkler system. It also said the hospital lacked detailed procedures and adequate training to deal with fires and other emergencies.The report said supervisory staff were not present when the fire broke out. Two nurses, a female security guard and a house officer were in the ward at the time.Emergency services were alerted six minutes after the fire started, while the first responders arrived 15 minutes after receiving the call, according to the interim report.Investigators also found that only two of the hospital's 13 standard operating procedures dealt with fires or other emergencies.“Those guilty of criminal negligence deserve no leniency,” Sharif was quoted as saying by the Associated Press. He ordered departmental and criminal proceedings against officials identified by the inquiry committee.Those facing action include the hospital's executive director, two joint executive directors, the head of the neonatal department, two doctors, the assistant director for security and the head of the Capital Development Authority's emergency services.Sharif also approved action against the private company responsible for hospital security and its officials.The government has announced compensation of 5 million Pakistani rupees (around $18,000) for each bereaved family.The interim report also recommended recognition for a nurse who risked her life to save a newborn before the flames spread through the ward. Sharif approved the recommendation to confer the Sitara-i-Khidmat, a state award for public service, on her.The deaths have triggered public anger and demands for accountability from grieving families and civil society groups.The incident has also prompted wider reviews of fire-safety arrangements at hospitals across Pakistan. Punjab authorities this week ordered an immediate assessment of fire-safety systems, firefighting equipment and emergency-response facilities at hospitals across the province.The fire was among Pakistan's deadliest recent tragedies involving children. In June, 14 schoolchildren were killed when the roof of an under-construction tutoring centre collapsed in Lahore.
Article Summary: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered the suspension of eight officials. He has also directed that criminal proceedings be initiated against those found responsible for a fire that killed 14 newborns at a hospital in Islamabad. The fire broke out on the third-floor nursery on Wednesday, where 15 newborns were being treated.

Article Title: Pakistan: Three missing men found dead with alleged torture marks in Balochistan
Article Text:
Representative file photo (IANS photo)

Three bodies recovered in Balochistan's Usta Muhammad have reportedly been identified as men who had earlier gone missing, with local sources alleging that they were forcibly disappeared after being detained by Pakistani security forces.According to The Balochistan Post, the deceased have been identified as Hafiz Mohammad Waqas, a Levies personnel from Machh in Bolan, his brother Mittha Khan, son of Nawab Khan, and Maqbool Ahmed, son of Jan Mohammad, a resident of Dasht Sabzband.Waqas was reportedly taken into custody and forcibly disappeared in May 2026. The three bodies were recovered from Usta Muhammad on August 24, according to local sources cited by the publication.The sources said the bodies bore apparent signs of torture. However, the circumstances surrounding their deaths have not been independently established, and no official findings from an investigation have been made public.The recoveries come amid reports of more than 15 bodies being found in different parts of Balochistan in recent days, including Panjgur, Mastung and Kharan. Several bodies recovered from Panjgur were allegedly identified as people who had previously been reported missing, while the identities of others remain unknown.The latest cases have renewed scrutiny of allegations of enforced disappearances in Balochistan, where rights groups and political organisations have for years raised concerns over the fate of missing people.Baloch political and human rights organisations have accused Pakistani security institutions of detaining people and, in some cases, killing them in custody before abandoning their bodies. Pakistan's authorities and security institutions have repeatedly denied involvement in enforced disappearances and allegations of extrajudicial killings.Rights groups and political organisations have called for credible and transparent investigations into the reported disappearances and deaths. They have also demanded that missing individuals be produced before courts, their families be informed of their whereabouts, and anyone accused of wrongdoing be subjected to due legal process.
Article Summary: Three bodies recovered in Balochistan's Usta Muhammad have reportedly been identified as men who had earlier gone missing. Local sources allege they were forcibly disappeared after being detained by Pakistani security forces. The circumstances surrounding their deaths have not been independently established, and no official findings from an investigation have been made public.

Article Title: 15 newborns killed in fire at Islamabad hospital's gynaecology ward in Pakistan
Article Text:
The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue sources.
